Account takeover fraud prevention: a bank playbook

MT

Mehak Tariq, CAMSNovember 24, 2026•8 min read

Account takeover fraud prevention is the set of controls that stops a criminal who has a customer's login details, or can trick the customer into giving them up, from taking over the account and moving money out. In practice that means stronger authentication at the moments attackers target, extra checks on credential resets and contact changes, monitoring that notices when an account stops behaving like its owner, and a response plan for the takeovers that get through. In a November 25, 2025 alert, the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) said that since January 2025 it "received more than 5,100 complaints reporting ATO fraud, with losses exceeding $262 million" (PSA I-112525-PSA).

This guide covers the controls and the team steps. It explains public guidance and is not legal advice.

How criminals get into the account

FinCEN's advisory FIN-2011-A016 sets account takeover apart from other computer intrusion because "the customer, rather than the financial institution maintaining the account, is the primary target." The FBI's account takeover page lists the usual ways in: brute forcing weak passwords on accounts without multi-factor authentication (MFA), phishing emails and lookalike login sites (including fake search ads, which it calls SEO poisoning), callers posing as bank staff who ask for a one-time passcode, credentials from past data breaches, and malware.

The 2025 PSA describes what follows. The criminal logs in, starts a password reset, and in "nearly all social engineering cases" locks the owner out. Money then leaves by wire, often to accounts "linked to cryptocurrency wallets". Bank staff are targets too: the FFIEC guidance says threat actors have deceived "customer call center and IT help desk representatives into resetting passwords and other credentials". FinCEN's 2024 analysis of identity-related suspicious activity found that "compromised credentials have a disproportionate financial impact as compared to other types of identity exploitation" (FinCEN).

What the FFIEC authentication guidance expects

The main supervisory text is the FFIEC's Authentication and Access to Financial Institution Services and Systems, issued August 11, 2021 (SR 21-14 at the Federal Reserve). It replaced the 2005 and 2011 internet banking guidance and endorses no specific security framework or standard. Four points in it shape an account takeover prevention program:

  • A current risk assessment, run "prior to implementing a new financial service, such as a faster payment product" and periodically after that, with input from fraud, customer service and cybersecurity. Data from actual fraud events can show which controls are ineffective.
  • Layered security that "incorporates multiple preventative, detective, and corrective controls", such as MFA, time-outs, monitoring and transaction amount limits.
  • Stronger authentication as risk rises. Single-factor authentication with layered security "has shown to be inadequate for customers engaged in high-risk transactions and for high-risk users." A customer starting a payment is one of its examples.
  • MFA or "controls of equivalent strength" where the risk assessment shows that is not enough.

It also covers call centers, customer education, and identity verification at account opening, which our guide to KYC verification explains.

Controls for each high-risk moment

This table maps each high-risk moment in the customer journey to example controls from the FFIEC appendix.

MomentWhat the attacker wantsExample controls in the FFIEC guidance
LoginUse stolen or phished credentialsMFA, unique passwords, prohibited password lists, rate limits on log-in attempts, lockout after repeated incorrect attempts, blocking devices or IP addresses linked to fraud
Password or credential resetGet staff to reset accessEnhanced authentication for resets, such as a one-time passcode to a pre-established device or a call-back to a pre-established phone number; flags for an unusual location or unidentifiable phone number; trained call center staff
Change of phone, email or deviceSend alerts and codes to the attackerEnhanced authentication for account maintenance, such as changes to email address, contact information or enrolled devices; processes for changed devices, "including changes to established phone numbers or carriers"
New payee or paymentMove funds out quicklyStronger authentication, restrictions on devices for adding payment recipients, transaction value limits, transaction alerts, fraud and anomaly monitoring
Business account administrationAdd a user or raise limitsExtra controls for the customer's system administrators, dual control, positive pay and debit blocks

The guidance warns that device cookies, geo-location and IP address matching "are considered insecure and ineffective if used alone", so treat them as one input among several. For business clients, positive pay lets the company reject items it did not issue. Dual control has limits too: the FBI describes criminals pressing the second approver to finish the transaction on the same fraudulent site.

Choosing MFA that holds up

CISA's phishing-resistant MFA fact sheet (October 2022) says some forms of MFA are vulnerable to phishing, "push bombing" attacks, SS7 protocol exploits and SIM swap attacks. The FFIEC adds that a one-time code can be intercepted, and the FBI tells customers that "MFA will not protect you if you land on a fraudulent login page." CISA ranks the options:

  • Phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO/WebAuthn or PKI-based), which CISA calls "the gold standard".
  • App-based one-time passcodes, or mobile push with number matching. CISA's number matching fact sheet recommends number matching against MFA fatigue where phishing-resistant MFA is not yet possible.
  • SMS or voice codes, which "should only be used as a last resort".

A bank that keeps SMS codes for customers who cannot use another method should give the change-of-phone controls more weight, because a SIM swap moves the phone number, and its codes, to the attacker.

AI in account takeover prevention

Treasury's March 2024 report on AI-specific cybersecurity risks in financial services says, from its interviews, that AI fraud detection tools "have been used by a wide range of financial institutions as part of risk management strategies for more than a decade". It also notes a data limit and a threat: firms reportedly share little fraud data, which restricts what models can learn, and institutions see AI impersonation of a customer's voice, video or behavior as "a chief concern". That matters because voice recognition and video chat are among the FFIEC's reset controls.

AI-based account takeover prevention builds on two control types in the FFIEC appendix: behavioral biometrics, which can use "finger swipes, taps, keystrokes, and mouse usage", and anomaly monitoring that watches transaction velocity and "increases in login or account lockout activity." A model that scores these inputs and holds payments should come under the bank's model risk management; our note on SR 26-2 covers the current model risk guidance.

How a bank team runs account takeover prevention, step by step

  1. Assess the risk. Run the account takeover risk assessment before each new channel or payment product and on a fixed cycle. Use the bank's own confirmed takeover cases to find the controls that failed.
  2. Map controls to the moments. For each row in the table, write down the authentication required, the step-up triggers and the limits, and who counts as high risk.
  3. Set the hold rules. Decide which combinations hold a payment, such as a new device, a phone number change and a new payee in one session, and who may release it.
  4. Verify through a trusted channel. Contact the customer through the phone number or device already on file, never one the caller or email supplies.
  5. Contain a confirmed takeover. End sessions, reset credentials, remove devices and payees the attacker added, and restore the contact details. Start a recall on any outgoing wire at once; the FBI tells victims to request a recall or reversal and report the wire to IC3. FinCEN's Rapid Response Program works with law enforcement and counterpart financial intelligence units to recover funds, and its FY 2025 year in review lists $21,121,807.94 frozen by partners in account takeover cases.
  6. Work the customer's claim. For consumer accounts, Regulation E's official interpretation says an unauthorized transfer "includes a transfer initiated by a person who obtained the access device from the consumer through fraud or robbery." Reg E does not cover transfers through Fedwire or a similar wire transfer system (12 CFR 1005.3(c)(3)), so these protections do not reach a stolen wire. Our Reg E guide covers liability limits and deadlines.
  7. File the SAR. 31 CFR 1020.320 covers suspicious transactions "conducted or attempted by, at, or through the bank" of at least $5,000 that meet its other conditions, filed within 30 calendar days of initial detection, or up to 30 more days if no suspect was identified. Money services businesses file under 31 CFR 1022.320, with a $2,000 threshold. The FinCEN SAR filing instructions (April 2026) list "Account takeover" at item 38a, and FinCEN's 2011 advisory asks for the term "account takeover fraud" in the narrative.
  8. Close the loop. Feed each case back into the risk assessment and customer education, and keep the record: alerts, contacts, holds, who decided and why, and the SAR decision.

In Verkflo's fraud alert triage use case, part of its AML automation, an AI agent gathers the device, login and transaction context for a flagged payment or account change, checks it against the team's rules and gives an analyst a recommendation, and the analyst decides.

Customer education that backs up the controls

The FFIEC describes a customer awareness program and warns that one not updated for new risks, "such as the introduction of a faster payments service", becomes ineffective. Its elements include how to recognize a real message from the bank, controls customers can turn on such as MFA, ways to monitor activity such as transaction alerts, who to call, and their Regulation E protections. The FBI's version for customers: use bookmarks for login pages, don't trust caller ID, and remember that "Companies generally do not contact you to ask for your username, password, or OTP."

Common questions

Does the FFIEC require MFA for every customer?

No. Each institution decides through its risk assessment, and the guidance points to MFA or controls of equivalent strength for high-risk transactions and users.

Is an SMS one-time passcode enough to prevent account takeover?

It beats a password alone, but CISA treats SMS as a last resort because of SIM swap and SS7 attacks, and a phishing site can capture any code a customer types. FIDO/WebAuthn holds up best.

Does a bank file a SAR when a takeover is blocked?

It may need to. The SAR rule covers attempted as well as conducted transactions, so a blocked transfer can be reportable when it meets the other conditions, including the $5,000 threshold. Record the decision either way.

What should a customer do right after a takeover?

The FBI says to contact the bank at once to request a recall or reversal, reset every exposed credential, and file a complaint at ic3.gov with the words "Account Takeover" in the description.

Sources

  • FFIEC, Authentication and Access to Financial Institution Services and Systems (August 11, 2021), and the Federal Reserve's SR 21-14
  • FinCEN Advisory FIN-2011-A016, Account Takeover Activity (December 19, 2011)
  • FinCEN Issues Analysis of Identity-Related Suspicious Activity (January 9, 2024)
  • FinCEN Year in Review for FY 2025
  • FinCEN SAR Filing Instructions (April 2026), 31 CFR 1020.320 and 31 CFR 1022.320
  • FBI IC3, Account Takeover Fraud via Impersonation of Financial Institution Support (November 25, 2025), and the IC3 account takeover page
  • CISA, Implementing Phishing-Resistant MFA and Implementing Number Matching in MFA Applications (October 2022)
  • US Treasury, Managing Artificial Intelligence-Specific Cybersecurity Risks in the Financial Services Sector (March 2024)
